title: Writing practice: Themes, methods, requests, and first flights
description: Eight writing tasks: argue a story's theme, compare ways to travel, tell a historical day as a narrative, interpret a poem, and write a respectful reply.

stimuli.title: Read: The Mural
paragraphs: Marisol had spent three weeks sketching the mural for the school wall. When the principal praised the design at the assembly, she smiled and said nothing about the others. Yet it was Kwame who had mixed every color until the blue matched the sky, and it was Dev and Alina who had stayed late to paint the high corners.

That night Marisol could not sleep. The next morning she asked the principal for a minute at the microphone. “The mural isn't only mine,” she said, her voice unsteady. “It exists because four people worked on it.”

Her face grew warm, but when Kwame grinned at her from the back row, the heaviness in her chest disappeared. Later, as the four of them stood before the finished wall, Marisol thought that the mural looked brighter than it had the day before.

stimuli.title: Two ways to find 15% of 60
paragraphs: Two students find 15% of 60.
Kai thinks: “10% of 60 is 6, and 5% of 60 is half of that, which is 3. So 15% of 60 is 6 + 3 = 9.”
Rosa thinks: “15% is the same as 0.15. So 0.15 × 60 = 9.”

stimuli.title: Getting around town: bus and bicycle
stimuli.caption: Facts that a city planner collected about two ways to travel across a town.
rows: Cost
$2 for each trip
Free to ride after you own or borrow a bicycle
Weather
Keeps riders dry in rain and snow
Riders get wet in rain and cold in snow
People
Can carry about 40 riders at one time
Carries one rider and a small bag
Schedule
Runs only at set times
Can leave any time the rider chooses

stimuli.title: Timeline: December 17, 1903
stimuli.caption: Facts about the first powered airplane flights, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
rows: Before the flights
Orville and Wilbur Wright had built a powered airplane. They brought it to the beach near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
First flight
Orville flew for 12 seconds and covered 120 feet (about 37 meters).
That day
The brothers took turns flying. They made four flights in all.
Last flight
Wilbur flew for 59 seconds and covered 852 feet (about 260 meters).
Afterward
A strong gust of wind flipped the airplane over and damaged it.

stimuli.title: Steps for a group presentation
stimuli.caption: Your class follows these four steps when a group prepares a presentation.
rows: 1. Choose roles
Each person takes a job, such as speaker, note-taker, or designer.
2. Divide the topic
Each person researches one part of the topic.
3. Practice together
The group presents once from beginning to end and listens to each other.
4. Ask for feedback
The group asks another group or the teacher what was clear and what was confusing.

stimuli.title: A draft slide
paragraphs: Your group is making a presentation about the water cycle. The group agreed on two rules: every slide must be easy to read from the back of the room, and the presentation must show all four stages (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection).

Your teammate Kai shares a draft slide in the group folder. The slide has the title “Water Cycle,” a paragraph of about 90 words in very small letters, and one picture of a cloud with rain. The picture has no labels. Kai writes, “What do you think of my slide?”

stimuli.title: A message in your group chat
paragraphs: You are working with three classmates on a science project that is due on Friday. Today, Jordan posted this message in your group chat:
“We have almost everything done. Let's skip tomorrow's practice session and just present on Friday. We already know the slides. It will save us time.”
You think the group should still practice. Last week, your group tried to present the slides and lost its place twice. Also, one slide had a spelling mistake that no one noticed.

stimuli.title: Poem: Moving Day
paragraphs: In this poem, the speaker has just moved to a new city.
The boxes stand like tall gray strangers in my room,
and the bare walls echo back my name.
Outside, the new street hums a tune I do not know.
My old street was a warm coat, worn soft at the elbows;
this one is stiff cardboard, folded the wrong way.
But when a neighbor's kid waves from a window,
a small light turns on in the middle of my chest,
a porch lamp, patient, in a house I have not entered.

items.stem: What lesson does this story teach? Write an argument that states the lesson (the theme) and proves it with at least two details from the story. Explain how each detail supports your idea.

checklist: I stated a theme as a complete idea, not just one word.
I used at least two details or short quotations from the story.
I explained how each detail supports the theme.
I showed how Marisol's choice or change helps show the theme.
I used academic language and connectors.
exemplar: States a theme as a full statement (for example, giving others credit makes success more meaningful)
Selects precise evidence (Marisol is silent at first, cannot sleep, speaks at the microphone, and the heaviness leaves her chest)
Explains how each detail supports the theme instead of only retelling
Traces the character's change from the beginning to the end
Uses academic language for literary analysis (theme, character, conflict, resolution) and integrates evidence smoothly

support.clue: Think about how Marisol feels at the beginning, what she decides, and how she feels at the end. What does her change teach readers?
support.frame: The lesson of this story is that ______. This is shown when ______. The text says, “______.” This detail shows that ______ because ______. Another important detail is ______, which proves ______. By the end, ______, which teaches readers that ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different story. “The lesson of this story is that patience can solve problems that anger cannot. This is shown when Leo waits quietly for his sister to finish talking. The text says, “He counted to ten and listened.” This detail shows that Leo chooses calm over anger because the argument ends peacefully. By the end, the family laughs together, which teaches readers that listening brings people closer.” Notice the theme as a full sentence and how each detail is explained. Analyze the mural story the same way.

items.stem: A classmate is stuck on 15% of 80 and asks which method to use. Write an argument that recommends one method, Kai's or Rosa's. Show how your method works with 80, and give reasons for your choice.

checklist: I recommended one method clearly.
I showed the steps of my method for 15% of 80 with correct numbers.
I gave at least two reasons for my choice.
I explained why the other method is also correct but not my choice.
I used math words such as percent, decimal, and multiply.
exemplar: Takes a clear position by recommending one method
Applies the method accurately: Kai's way gives 8 + 4 = 12, and Rosa's way gives 0.15 × 80 = 12
Gives reasons for the choice (for example, fewer steps, easier mental math, or works with any number)
Acknowledges that both methods are valid and compares them
Uses mathematical vocabulary and justification language (because, since, therefore)

support.clue: First try both methods on 15% of 80 so you know both give the same answer. Then think about which one is easier for your classmate and why.
support.frame: I recommend ______ method because ______. For 15% of 80, ______. This gives ______. Another reason is ______. Although ______ method also works because ______, ______. Therefore, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different choice. “I recommend counting by tens for finding the total of 7 bags with 10 apples each. Counting by tens gives 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, so the total is 70. Another reason is that I can check my work quickly. Although multiplying 7 × 10 also works because it gives the same total, counting by tens helps me see the pattern. Therefore, I recommend counting by tens.” Notice the recommendation, a worked example, and the reasons. Do the same for 15% of 80.

items.stem: A new student asks how people get around your town. Write a paragraph that compares the bus and the bicycle. Tell how they are different, tell one way they are alike, and use at least three features from the table.

checklist: I wrote a topic sentence that names both ways to travel.
I compared at least three features from the table.
I used contrast words such as but, while, whereas, and in contrast.
I told one way they are alike.
I used accurate facts.
exemplar: Topic sentence introduces both ways to travel and the purpose of the comparison
Compares at least three features accurately (for example, $2 or free, about 40 riders or one rider, set times or any time)
Uses contrast connectors (while, whereas, in contrast, however) and a similarity expression (both, like)
Organizes the paragraph feature by feature rather than listing each way separately
Ends with a closing statement that sums up the comparison

support.clue: Go through the table one row at a time. For each feature, ask how the bus and the bicycle are different. Then think of one way they are the same.
support.frame: The bus and the bicycle are both ______, but they are different in several ways. In terms of cost, the bus ______, whereas the bicycle ______. Also, the bus ______ while the bicycle ______. In contrast, ______. One way they are alike is ______.
support.model: Mentor example about different things. “A tent and a cabin are both places to sleep outdoors, but they are different in several ways. In terms of weight, a tent can be carried in a bag, whereas a cabin cannot be moved. Also, a tent is quick to set up, while a cabin must be built. In contrast, a cabin keeps out the cold better. One way they are alike is that both give shelter.” Notice the contrast words and the final similarity. Compare the bus and the bicycle the same way.

facts: The cost, weather, capacity, and schedule details are illustrative facts supplied in the table.

items.stem: Write a historical narrative that tells the story of this day in the order it happened. Use details from the timeline, and help your reader picture the events.

checklist: I told the events in the correct order.
I used at least four details from the timeline.
I used time words and past-tense verbs.
I wrote it as a story with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
exemplar: Organizes the story in chronological order with transitions (first, later, by the end of the day)
Uses facts accurately (12 seconds and 120 feet, four flights, 59 seconds and 852 feet, the wind gust)
Uses past tense and varied sentence beginnings
Adds concrete detail that shows why the day mattered
Has a clear beginning, middle, and end, with a closing thought about the day

support.clue: Read the timeline from top to bottom. Decide which details belong in the beginning, which in the middle, and which in the ending of your story.
support.frame: On December 17, 1903, ______ and ______ went to ______. At first, ______. Then ______. Later that day, ______. Wilbur’s last flight lasted ______ and covered ______. At the end of the day, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different event. “On Friday, the actors gathered backstage before the school play. At first, everyone felt nervous. Then the curtain opened, and the first scene began. Later, the audience clapped for a long time. At the end of the day, the cast agreed that all the practice had been worth it.” Notice the time words that move the story forward. Tell the story of this day the same way.

facts: On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered airplane flights near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
The first flight, by Orville, lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet (about 37 meters).
The brothers made four flights that day; the last, by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet (about 260 meters).
After the flights, a gust of wind flipped the airplane and damaged it.

items.stem: A new student has just joined your class and will do a group presentation next week. Write a clear explanation of how the group should prepare. Explain what happens in each step and why that step helps the group.

checklist: I explained all four steps in order.
I gave a reason for each step using because, so that, or in order to.
I used sequence words such as first, second, after that, and finally.
I used a friendly, helpful tone suited to a new classmate.
I used precise words such as roles, feedback, and practice.
exemplar: Covers all four steps in the correct order with sequencing words
Explains the purpose of each step (for example, roles prevent confusion, dividing the topic shares the work, practice reveals problems, feedback improves clarity)
Uses purpose and cause language (so that, in order to, because) accurately
Uses an audience-aware, helpful tone and precise task vocabulary
Organizes the response with an introduction and a closing sentence

support.clue: For each step, answer two questions: what does the group do, and what problem does this step help avoid? Use the words in the table as your starting point.
support.frame: To prepare for a group presentation, first, ______ so that ______. Second, ______ because ______. After that, ______ in order to ______. Finally, ______ so that ______. If the group follows these steps, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different process. “To get ready for a science lab, first, students read the directions so that they know the steps. Second, they collect the materials because the lab cannot start without them. After that, they put on goggles in order to protect their eyes. Finally, they begin the experiment so that they can record the results. If students follow these steps, the lab runs safely.” Notice that each step has a reason. Explain the presentation steps the same way.

items.stem: Write feedback to Kai. Say whether the slide is ready for the presentation, give at least two reasons that use details about the slide, and suggest one change. Use kind, respectful language.

checklist: I began with a friendly greeting and thanked Kai.
I said clearly whether the slide is ready.
I gave at least two reasons using details about the slide and the group’s rules.
I suggested one change that would help.
I used kind, respectful language and ended with a question or an offer to help.
exemplar: Opens kindly and states a clear judgment (for example, the slide is not ready yet)
Gives two or more reasons tied to the slide details and the group’s rules (small letters and a long paragraph are hard to read from the back; the picture shows only rain, so not all four stages)
Suggests a concrete change (shorter text, larger letters, a labeled diagram of all four stages)
Uses polite feedback language (I think, it might help, could we) and modal verbs
Keeps a respectful tone suited to a message to a teammate

support.clue: Compare the slide with the group’s two rules. Which details help, and which details cause a problem?
support.frame: Hi Kai, thanks for sharing your slide. I think the slide ______. One reason is that ______. Another reason is that ______. I suggest ______ so that ______. What do you think?
support.model: Mentor example about a different draft. “Hi Mia, thanks for sharing your poster. I think the poster is almost ready. One reason is that the title is large and easy to read. Another reason is that the picture matches the topic. However, the labels are very small. I suggest making the labels bigger so that people can read them from the back of the room. What do you think?” Notice the kind start, the reasons, and the suggestion. Write your feedback to Kai the same way.

facts: The water cycle includes stages such as evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.

items.stem: Write a reply to Jordan in the group chat. Disagree respectfully, give at least two reasons based on what happened last week, answer Jordan's idea about saving time, and suggest a plan that the group can agree on.

checklist: I started politely and showed that I understand Jordan's idea.
I disagreed respectfully using phrases such as I see your point, but.
I gave two reasons based on what happened last week.
I answered Jordan's point about saving time.
I suggested a plan the group can agree on.
exemplar: Shows respect by acknowledging Jordan's concern before disagreeing (I understand that..., however...)
Uses specific evidence from the scenario (the group lost its place twice, and a spelling mistake was missed)
Responds to the time concern with reasoning, such as a short practice that prevents mistakes
Proposes a compromise plan with concrete details
Uses modal verbs and contrast structures (could, should, although, however) in a register suited to a respectful group chat

support.clue: Show Jordan you listened before you disagree. Then use the two things that happened last week as proof. Finally, think of a plan that gives Jordan something too.
support.frame: Hi Jordan, I understand that ______. However, I think we should still ______ because ______. For example, last week ______. Also, ______. I agree that ______, so maybe we could ______. That way, ______. What do you think?
support.model: Mentor example about a different disagreement. “Hi Maya, I understand that you want to finish the poster tonight. However, I think we should still check the facts because mistakes are easy to miss. For example, yesterday we wrote the wrong date on our timeline. Also, our teacher grades accuracy. I agree that we are short on time, so maybe we could check the facts in ten minutes. That way, we can finish tonight and be sure the poster is correct. What do you think?” Notice the polite start, the evidence, and a compromise. Write your reply to Jordan the same way.

items.stem: Explain how the poet uses figurative language to show how the speaker feels about moving. Choose two comparisons from the poem, explain what each one means, and explain how the speaker's feelings change.

checklist: I chose two comparisons from the poem and quoted or named them.
I explained what each comparison means in plain words.
I explained what feeling each comparison shows.
I explained how the feelings change by the end of the poem.
I used literary words such as simile, metaphor, and tone.
exemplar: Identifies figurative language accurately (for example, the simile boxes like tall gray strangers, or the metaphors the old street was a warm coat and a porch lamp)
Interprets each comparison (strangers suggest something unfamiliar and cold, a warm coat suggests comfort, a porch lamp suggests welcome and hope)
Links the language to the speaker's feelings: loneliness at first, then growing hope
Traces the change from the first lines to the last lines
Uses literary terms (simile, metaphor, tone) accurately and explains the evidence instead of only quoting it

support.clue: Look for phrases that compare one thing to another, such as those with like or was a. Ask what each thing is like and what feeling it brings. Then compare the first lines with the last lines.
support.frame: In the poem, the poet uses ______ to show that the speaker feels ______. For example, the line “______” compares ______ to ______. This suggests that ______. In contrast, the line “______” shows ______. By the end of the poem, the speaker feels ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different poem. “In this poem, the poet uses a metaphor to show that the speaker feels calm. For example, the line “the evening was a quiet lake” compares the evening to a lake. This suggests that nothing is disturbing the speaker. In contrast, the line “my worries were small waves” shows that the speaker's problems no longer seem big. By the end of the poem, the speaker feels peaceful because the worries have faded.” Notice the quotation, what it compares, and what feeling it suggests. Explain your poem the same way.

facts: A simile compares two things using like or as; a metaphor says that one thing is another.
The poem is original text supplied in the stimulus.
